newsitem.title: UK: European grains quiet, no EU tender.
newsitem.headline: European grains quiet, no EU tender.

text.p: European grain markets went into a pre-holiday lull this week, helped by the fact that there is no EU grain tender.
Aggressive EU exporting over recent months means that Europe could be left with a relaxed final three months to the season, despite a large crop.
French wheat prices held steady this week as buyers and sellers kept to the sidelines and business slowed down sharply ahead of the Easter holidays, dealers said.
Wheat prices had firmed last Friday after nearly 500,000 tonnes of wheat were awarded at the EU tender, and then held at that level throughout this week.
Maize prices were unchanged on the week but barley prices were firmer, dealers said.
There was little fresh export news to move wheat, dealers said.
Wheat prices were likely to remain firm because exporters still face heavy loading schedules in ports, they said.
April wheat into Rouen was bid at 895 francs per tonne and offered at 900 francs, unchanged on last Friday.
On the export front Algeria bought 75,000 tonnes of European Union wheat for April/May shipment. One trader said it was almost certain the wheat would come from France.
But exporters largely ignored the news, particularly after reports Canada and Australia made hefty wheat sales on world markets.
They said this indicated that while the European Union may still manage to sell its wheat to nearby countries, it had lost its competitive edge on other destinations.
"This confirms that at current European price levels, there can only be business with nearby markets," one dealer said.

There were trade reports that India bought at least one million tonnes of Australian wheat and that Canada sold over 500,000 tonnes of wheat to Iran and more than 100,000 tonnes of wheat to the Philippines.

April-June barley into Rouen was paid at 850 francs per tonne, against 840 francs last week. Dealers said two large trading houses have turned buyers, possibly in anticipation of a return of Saudi Arabia to the world market. But there was still no confirmation that a tender was in the pipeline.
German wheat prices held steady on the strength of recent business but there were no new orders in the run-up to the holidays, brokers said.
"We're carrying out old deals but both supply and demand have been shrinking since last week," one said.
"Co-ops and merchants stocks are looking thinner and there is no fresh export demand."
"But domestic millers may come into the market in April to look for June and third quarter supply ahead of the new crop."
Relatively high wheat export allocations last week in Brussels included grain aimed at North Africa, the Middle East and the former Soviet Union, traders said.
Some 75,000 tonnes of German wheat featured among the 480,000 tonnes granted. This should keep wheat away from intervention stores which reported sizeable offers of feed barley and rye.

In the UK, a currency induced fall in prices put more life into a quiet pre-holiday market. Despite the fall, traders' attitude is bullish, especially on exports, with some taking the view that the UK has pretty well exported as much as it needs to for the current campaign, and predicting a tighter market for the final three months.

"Everybody's figures are different," one trader said. "We may have 200,000 tonnes (of exports) left to do, or we may have nothing," he said. How tight the market would be from now on depended on the detail of what the exact crop size was and on exactly what compounders are doing. Both are unknowns, he said.
The UK has a steady stream of exports to non-EU countries, with vessels recently loaded, loading or shortly to load for, for example, China, Tunisia and Sri Lanka.
Spain remained preoccupied with the lack of rain, which is pressuring cereal prices higher both in the southern region and in the rest of the country, traders said.
"In the north we've started to see farmers holding back supplies for fear of a lower harvest if the weather doesn't improve," said one Madrid dealer.
"If the dry weather continues, we're going to have problems with all of the crops, if not in terms of quantity then at least in terms of quality," he added.
Maize and durum wheat trade was quiet, with a lack of both buyers and sellers. But offered maize prices were higher in sympathy with other grains, traders said.

Italian durum wheat prices rose slightly over the past week as demand was slightly firmer and producers have been reluctant to sell, the Italian Institute for Agriculture Studies said. Ismea noted that the increase in foreign durum wheat prices also had a negative impact on the local market.
Trade has been thin because of the upcoming Easter holidays, Italian traders said.
